After Apple unveiled changes to App Tracking Transparency in Europe, the company is now introducing a simplified App Store commission structure for developers in the region. Here are the details.

Apple overhauls business terms for EU app developers

Apple previously announced eight adjustments to its App Tracking Transparency features in Europe, made in response to an investigation by Germany's antitrust regulator.

Apple has now announced that a new commission structure will take effect on October 1 in Europe, including cutting the external link commission to 15% and replacing the controversial Core Technology Fee with a 5% Core Technology Commission.

This move comes more than a year after Apple announced major reforms to the EU App Store, which introduced a series of complex rules — you can learn more about that here.

Below is Apple's statement:

Apple also announced new terms for App Store commission rates, alternative app payment options, and the distribution of apps through alternative app marketplaces or the web.

The new terms are as follows:

App Store apps using Apple's in-app purchase system will have a commission of 26%. For the vast majority of developers — including those in the App Store Small Business Programme, Mini Apps Partner Programme, or Video Partner Programme, as well as auto-renewing subscriptions after the first year — the commission will be 15%. For App Store apps using alternative payment processing, the commission will be 20%. Developers in the aforementioned programmes will be eligible for the lower 10% rate. For App Store apps that direct users externally to a website to complete a transaction, the commission will be 15%. Developers in the aforementioned programmes will pay the lower 10% rate. For apps distributed through alternative app marketplaces or the web, Apple will charge a 5% Core Technology Commission.

Under the new terms, developers can also offer both Apple's in-app purchase system and alternative payment options, whether in-app or via an external link to a website, as long as they meet Apple's "presentation requirements" and maintain their chosen payment option for 12 months.

Today's announcement also includes new child safety protections and alternative payment arrangements in the EU, including:

Apps in the App Store's "Kids" category will not contain links that direct users externally to a website to complete a transaction, in order to reduce the risk of scams or fraud targeting children. For users under 18, all App Store apps that use alternative payment processing or external links to websites for transactions must include parental controls requiring younger users to have a parent or guardian's involvement before making a purchase. For users under 13, apps on the App Store cannot direct users externally to a website for transactions, in order to prevent the risk of scams targeting young children.

Apple added that in EU member states where children above a certain age are required to have parental consent for digital activities, "these protections will be adjusted accordingly."

Finally, Apple's latest announced changes also expand eligibility for operating alternative app marketplaces or distributing apps via the web.

The expanded eligibility criteria include:

Meeting a moderate financial stability threshold as rated by Dun & Bradstreet. Being a publicly traded company or owned by one. Having received venture capital funding from a recognised investment institution. Having completed a financial audit by a licensed accounting firm. Being a government agency, educational institution, or non-profit organisation.

Apple pointed out that the web distribution method currently available only in the EU lacks the ongoing oversight provided by marketplace operators, which could allow bad actors to "operate for a long time before being discovered, harming users."

Therefore, Apple said it will continue to require that all apps distributed through alternative channels must go through its Notarisation process.

To learn more about today's announcement, please visit this link.

Update: In a statement to Bloomberg, a European Commission spokesperson said it welcomed Apple's changes, noting they were the result of "close dialogue" with the company. The spokesperson added that the Commission will monitor how Apple implements the new terms.

What are your thoughts on Apple's new rules in the EU? Feel free to share them in the comments section.
